97b36f8c93:
Chapter 1 gave you names, objects, and references. This chapter turns that machinery into the tool you will reach for most: the function. A function packages a computation under a name so you write it once and use it everywhere. The ideas here show up in every Python program you will ever read:

  • how arguments bind to parameters,
  • how names resolve across scopes,
  • how functions remember their surroundings.

Decorators, callbacks, and frameworks you have not met yet all rest on them.
e8b49d9371: Common mistakes here are small but worth naming. The classic is forgetting return and then wondering why a variable is None. Another is writing return inside a loop when you meant to collect results. The early return fires on the first iteration, and the loop never finishes. When a function unexpectedly gives None, check two things. Is there a return on every path that should produce a value? And is a return firing earlier than you meant?
c7cc673161: Use early returns to flatten nested logic. Instead of indenting the whole body inside if valid:, return immediately when the input is invalid. The main path then sits at the left margin. That shape reads better, and it is the reason early returns exist. Do not use a function where a plain expression will do. Wrapping one line in def adds a name you must remember for no gain.
2355a54dcd: A realistic case: boolean flags. register(7, "Awanish", True) leaves the reader guessing what True means. Make the flag keyword-only and the call becomes register(7, "Awanish", notify=True). Now every call site shows the flag's purpose. Nobody can silently pass it positionally in the wrong slot. Positional-only fits the other end: an id or a path whose name callers should never depend on. If you later rename user_id to account_id, positional callers keep working.
fc4e621796: Some arguments are usually the same. A timeout is usually 30 seconds; a retry count is usually 3. Default values let callers omit the boring arguments and name only what changes. The syntax is name=value in the def line. Parameters with defaults must come after parameters without them. Otherwise a positional call could not know which parameter a value belongs to.
6e631809fc: The standard fix is the None sentinel: default to None, then build the real object inside the body. Each call gets its own list. Callers can still pass their own list, and that keeps working exactly as before. Sometimes None itself is a meaningful value for the parameter. That is rare, but it happens. Then use a private sentinel object instead: _unset = object(), and default to that. Same idea, no ambiguity.
372ba20b57: Diagnosing this bug: the symptom is state leaking between calls. The function behaves differently the second time with the same inputs. When you see that, look at the def line first. The fix is mechanical: replace the mutable default with None and construct inside. After fixing, re-run the same two calls back to back. The leak disappears.
15d4fa3551: Sometimes you cannot name every parameter in advance. A report builder takes any number of sections. A decorator must forward whatever arguments the wrapped function takes. *args and **kwargs are the language's answer. In a parameter list, *args collects all extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects all extra keyword arguments into a dict. The names args and kwargs are convention; the stars are what matter.
eaa2ff94eb: The common mistake is overusing them. When the parameter set is known, name it. def connect(host, port, timeout) tells the reader everything. def connect(*args, **kwargs) tells them nothing, breaks tab-completion, and hides errors until deep inside the body. Reserve *args/**kwargs for genuinely open-ended signatures and for forwarding wrappers. A middle ground exists. Accept the known parameters explicitly, and add **kwargs only for forward-compatible options. Just document what those options are.
0299629ddb:
The second and first calls are identical. The call site unpacking just moved where the values were assembled. The binding order is strict and worth memorizing:

  1. positional arguments fill parameters left to right,
  2. then keyword arguments fill by name,
  3. then defaults fill whatever is left.

A parameter that gets two values — one positional, one keyword — raises TypeError instead of guessing.
ad65fd930f: Reading a name searches outward. Writing a name is a different rule, and it trips up almost everyone once. Any assignment to a name inside a function body makes that name local to the whole function body, unless you declare otherwise. Python decides this at compile time, before the function ever runs. So reading the name before the assignment line finds a local name with nothing bound to it yet. The result is UnboundLocalError, not NameError. That error message tells you exactly what happened: the name is local, it just has no value yet.
937560b46e: Three sharp edges. First, global on a name that does not exist yet at module level creates it on first assignment. It does not require a prior binding, which surprises people. Second, nonlocal does require the name to exist in an enclosing function scope. Otherwise you get a SyntaxError at definition time. That is actually helpful: it fails fast. Third, UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError, so a bare except NameError catches it. When debugging, catch or print the specific subclass so you know which rule you hit.
d1c6009e62:
Practical uses go beyond counters:

  • callbacks that remember their context (each button handler remembering its index),
  • decorator factories that remember configuration,
  • small state machines.

Sometimes the state grows past a couple of variables, or needs methods with names. Then a class becomes clearer. Closures are for small, focused memory.

One more caution: closures keep their enclosing scope alive. A closure stored in a long-lived registry pins every variable in that scope. That can hold large objects in memory longer than you meant. If a closure only needs one small value, do not build it inside a scope holding a huge one.
c6fb0cc4e6: Functions are objects — full citizens. You can store them in lists and dicts, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. A function that takes or returns another function is a higher-order function. A lambda is simply a compact way to write a small one. lambda x: x + 1 is a function of one parameter. Its body is the single expression after the colon. It is not a weaker kind of function. It just cannot contain statements.
8f92b65222: Use lambda for throwaway one-expression functions: sort keys, short predicates, simple callbacks. Use def for anything reused, anything with statements, and anything whose logic deserves a name. Your own higher-order functions may take a function argument. Name that parameter after its role — key, predicate, handler — so callers know what kind of function to pass.
7c3b388419: Two hard limits. Each call consumes stack space, and Python caps the depth: exceed it and you get RecursionError. The cap is readable via sys.getrecursionlimit(), and it is 1000 by default in CPython. Treat that number as a CPython implementation detail, not a language guarantee. Other implementations may differ, and the language specification does not fix it. Also note that CPython does not optimize tail calls. A recursion a thousand deep is a thousand live frames, no matter how you write it.
6f7285237c: When recursion helps: tree-shaped and nested data, such as directory walks, nested JSON, and expression trees. The code follows the data's shape and reads naturally. When iteration is clearer: linear sequences, counting, anything deep. If the depth can grow with the input size, recursion is the wrong tool. A list nested 10,000 deep needs a loop. And when a recursive solution repeats subproblems, as Fibonacci does, either memoize or go iterative.
7ed98da558: Solution 5 — code/ch02/ex-14.py. The base case: an item that is not a list is appended directly. That branch never recurses, so the descent always ends. The iterative version keeps its own stack instead of using the call stack. So the recursion limit puts no cap on its depth.
928dc70c23: Solution 4 — code/ch02/ex-13.py. balance lives in make_account's scope; both inner functions rebind it with nonlocal. Each make_account call creates a fresh balance. So accounts are independent by construction. There is no shared name for them to collide on.
